title: The Mystery of the Missing Buoys
markdown:
The sun, a molten gold coin, kissed the river. Rhea, coxswain with eyes sharper than any hawk, scanned the water. Her team’s buoys — bright orange beacons — had vanished. Poof. Gone. Coach Davies ran a hand over his bald head. “Unprecedented,” he declared. Practice was off.

“Unprecedented,” Rhea whispered to Splinter, her gull. A shiver of excitement, not fear, jolted her. A mystery. Then the familiar whisper: what if you fail? She grabbed the dinghy anyway. “We’ll find them.”

Splinter, a feathered scout, spotted a subtle ripple, a trail of uprooted reeds snaking downstream. They followed. The dinghy darted. Ducks scattered, squawking. A peculiar swirl tugged them toward a gnarled ancient tree.

Splinter cried out, sharp. A flash of brilliant orange hung on a submerged branch by the old derelict mill. They nudged closer. The missing buoys were a tangled mess, pulled by a powerful undertow toward the mill’s dark maw. “The mill,” Rhea said, voice tight. “That current is dragging them in.”

A gruff voice boomed from the crumbling doorway. “Hey. What are you doing there? Trespassing.” Old Mr. Silas shuffled out, his face a roadmap of frowns.

“We’re looking for our rowing buoys,” Rhea said. Her heart thumped.

Silas grumbled. “Securing things that drift in. Can’t have folks getting hurt.” He gestured to a section of wall that sagged. The planks groaned. He was the reason the buoys were missing, and he was not about to hand them over for a smile and a club badge. The team’s chances were slipping with the current.

Rhea watched him. She saw the lonely circuit of his days, the way his eyes darted to that crumbling wall. Panic urged her to snatch the buoys and bolt. Silas was not a villain. He was a man trying to keep his world from falling apart.

“Mr. Silas,” she said, clear and steady, “I can help. My team, we’re strong. We know how to brace things. If you let us have the buoys, I’ll help you fix that wall. Properly.”

Silas blinked. He looked at Rhea, then at the sag. He grumbled, but a flicker of hope sparked. “You think you can?”

Rhea took the lead. Splinter pinpointed the weakest spots. They used the dinghy’s oars as makeshift levers. Silas, grudging, joined. An unlikely crew, they reinforced the wall.

As the sun descended in orange and purple, the mill stood more securely. Silas’s frown lines softened. He managed a small genuine smile. “Alright, lass. You’ve earned them.” He helped heave the tangled buoys into the dinghy.

The next morning the river gleamed. The buoys bobbed in their rightful places. Rhea and Splinter stood at the stern of the racing shell. The River Rapids rowed with a powerful synchronized rhythm. Coach Davies, for once, did not say unprecedented. Splinter gave a contented squawk. Rhea called the stroke and did not look back at the empty water. It was not empty anymore.
